blocks.text: XML generation asks a model to structure its output using named opening and closing tags, an alternative to JSON, covered in the previous topic, that some tasks and some models handle especially well, particularly for longer, document style structured content.

This topic covers how XML tag structure differs from JSON, why explicit named tags can be easier for a model to keep correctly balanced than JSON braces, when XML is the better structured format choice, and how to extract data from an XML formatted response.
1. What XML Generation Means

blocks.alt: Building on JSON generation, XML generation uses named tag structure

blocks.text: XML generation structures output using named tags, an opening tag and a matching closing tag wrapping the actual content, name and closing name, rather than the brace and bracket syntax JSON uses.
2. XML Tags vs JSON Braces

blocks.alt: JSON uses braces and brackets, XML uses named opening and closing tags

blocks.text: Where JSON identifies structure through braces, brackets, and quoted keys, XML identifies structure through named tags that explicitly state what they are, a tag literally spells out its own name at both the open and close, making the structure more directly readable even without special formatting.
3. Why Named Tags Can Stay More Reliably Balanced

blocks.alt: An opening tag, content inside, and a matching closing tag form one complete unit

blocks.text: Because each XML tag names itself explicitly at both open and close, name and closing name, a model generating XML has an easier time keeping track of exactly what needs to close and when, compared to JSON generic braces and brackets, which carry no explicit label about what they are closing.
4. Nesting With Explicit Open and Close Structure

blocks.alt: An outer tag contains inner tag A and inner tag B nested within it

blocks.text: Nested XML structure follows the same explicit tagging pattern at every level, an outer tag wraps one or more inner tags, each with its own clear open and close, making even fairly deep nesting relatively easy to visually follow compared to counting matching braces in JSON.
5. XML for Long-Form Structured Content

blocks.alt: Short, flat structured data is compared against long form document or report content

blocks.text: XML tends to shine particularly for longer, document style content, a report with clearly labeled sections, a multi part response where each part deserves its own explicit label, JSON generally remains the more common choice for short, flat, data centric structures.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Content Type","Better Fit"],"rows":[["Short, flat key-value data","JSON"],["Long form, sectioned document content","XML"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Extracting Data From XML Output

blocks.alt: XML output gets parsed by matching tag names, extracting field values

blocks.text: An application receiving XML output parses it by locating specific tag names and extracting the content between their open and close, most programming languages have XML parsing libraries just as mature as their JSON equivalents, making this extraction reliable in practice.

code.content:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

root = ET.fromstring(model_response)
name = root.find("name").text
email = root.find("email").text

blocks.text: 7. Anthropic Models and XML Tag Conventions

blocks.title: This is a genuinely documented, real world convention
blocks.content: Anthropic documentation for Claude models specifically recommends XML style tags for structuring both prompts and requested outputs, since Claude models have been trained with particular attention to this convention, making XML an especially reliable choice when working with that model family.

blocks.text: This is covered in much greater detail in the later Anthropic APIs module, but it is worth knowing early that XML tagging is not just a generic structured format choice, it is a specifically well supported convention for certain model families.
8. Common XML Formatting Issues

blocks.alt: Mismatched opening and closing tags produce invalid XML structure

blocks.text: The most common XML formatting error is a mismatched tag, an opening tag whose corresponding closing tag uses the wrong name or is missing entirely, this breaks parsing exactly the way a missing brace breaks JSON, validating the actual output remains just as important here as with JSON.
9. XML vs JSON, Choosing Between Them

For most short, data centric extraction tasks, JSON remains the more broadly convenient default, for longer, more document like structured content, or when working specifically with a model family known to handle XML tagging especially well, XML becomes the stronger choice.
Worked Example

A developer generating a structured multi section report using JSON finds the output occasionally breaks due to unescaped quote characters within long text fields, a formatting fragility that becomes more likely as content length grows.

Switching to XML tags for the same report structure, wrapping each section in its own clearly named tag, produces more consistently well formed output for this longer, document style content, since the explicit named tags give the model a clearer structural anchor to maintain across a longer generation.
Common Mistakes

items: Defaulting to JSON for every task without considering XML for longer, document style structured content
Not validating that opening and closing tags actually match before attempting to parse the response
Assuming every model handles XML tagging equally well without checking model specific documentation and conventions
Over nesting XML structure unnecessarily for what is really just simple, flat data better suited to JSON

blocks.text: Practice

Take a structured extraction task you have previously done with JSON, rewrite the same request using XML tags instead, and compare how each format handles a longer piece of text content within one of the fields.
Key Takeaway

XML generation structures output with explicitly named opening and closing tags, offering an advantage over JSON for longer, document style content and for model families specifically well suited to this convention, while JSON generally remains the more convenient default for short, flat, data centric structures.
